definition:
The incarnation is the church's confession that the eternal Son of God, without ceasing to be God, became a man, Jesus of Nazareth, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He did not stop being God to become man, nor did he merely appear human, nor was a good man later adopted into divine status. One and the same person, the Son, who shares the Father's life from eternity, took to himself a complete human nature, body and soul, mind and will, and lived a real human life. John's Gospel says it in four Greek words: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon in 451 set the boundaries of the confession: one person in two natures, fully divine and fully human, the natures neither mixed nor changed, neither divided nor separated. This study traces how Scripture comes to say this; the doctrine of the Trinity, the promises of the Messiah, and the resurrection of Jesus have their own studies, and the site's page on who Jesus is sets out the ancient alternatives in detail.

The word comes from the Latin incarnatio, from caro, ‘flesh’, translating the Greek of John 1:14, ho logos sarx egeneto, ‘the Word became flesh’. In the Bible sarx, ‘flesh’, can mean the body, human nature in its weakness and mortality, or (in Paul) human life in rebellion against God; in John 1:14 it means full human existence in its frailty. The same verse says the Word ‘pitched his tent’ among us (skēnoō, from skēnē, ‘tent’), the word the Septuagint used for the tabernacle, God's dwelling in Israel's camp. Paul's hymn in Philippians 2 says Christ, existing in the ‘form’ (morphē) of God, ‘emptied himself’ (kenoō, from which comes the theological word kenosis), taking the form of a servant and being made in human ‘likeness’ (homoiōma). The Nicene Creed of 325 and 381 used two verbs, sarkōthenta, ‘was made flesh’ or ‘incarnate’, and enanthrōpēsanta, ‘became man’, to shut out any reading in which the Son only wore a body. Chalcedon's key terms were physis, ‘nature’, what a thing is, and hypostasis or prosōpon, ‘person’, who a thing is.
ot:
The Old Testament does not predict the incarnation in so many words. What it does is create the expectation that God himself will come and dwell with his people, and plant promises about a coming king that strain the categories of ordinary humanity. Its opening chapters already set up a tension. God is not a creature and cannot be pictured: at Sinai Israel “saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12), and God tells Moses, “no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Yet God is not absent from his world. He walks in the garden, appears to Abraham at Mamre among three visitors in human form (Genesis 18:1-2), wrestles with Jacob (Genesis 32:24-30), and speaks from the burning bush as “the angel of the LORD” (Exodus 3:2), a figure who is sometimes distinct from God and sometimes speaks as God. Manoah, after the angel ascends in the altar flame, says, “we have seen God” (Judges 13:22). Many church fathers, from Justin Martyr in the second century onward, read these appearances as the Son acting before his incarnation; many modern interpreters read them as God's self-manifestation through an angelic messenger. Either way, they show God making himself present in visible, even human, form without ceasing to be the invisible God.

The dominant Old Testament picture is God's dwelling. God commands a sanctuary “so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8), and when the tabernacle is complete, “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Solomon, dedicating the temple, asks the question the incarnation will answer: “But will God indeed dwell upon the earth?” (1 Kings 8:27). Ezekiel sees the glory leave the temple before the Babylonian destruction and promises a day when “My dwelling place will be with them” (Ezekiel 37:27); in his inaugural vision he sees on the heavenly throne “a figure like that of a man” (Ezekiel 1:26). Isaiah announces to exiled Jerusalem, “Here is your God” (Isaiah 40:9), and a voice cries to prepare in the wilderness the way for the LORD himself (Isaiah 40:3). Malachi promises that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” (Malachi 3:1). The Gospels apply both Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1 to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus, so that the one who comes after John is the LORD who comes.

The royal promises move in the same direction. A king from David's line is called God's son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), and Psalm 45:6 addresses the king, “Your throne, O God, endures forever”, a verse Hebrews 1:8 applies to the Son. Isaiah 7:14 promises a sign to the faithless king Ahaz: the ‘almah, a Hebrew word for a young woman of marriageable age, will bear a son called Immanuel, ‘God with us’. The Septuagint rendered ‘almah with parthenos, ‘virgin’, and Matthew 1:23 quotes that Greek form. Interpreters differ on whether Isaiah's sign had a first fulfillment in Ahaz's day, as the context of Isaiah 7 and 8 suggests to many, with Matthew seeing its fullest meaning in Jesus, or whether it was a direct prophecy of the virgin birth alone; Jewish interpreters have generally read it of a child born in Isaiah's own time. Two chapters later a child is born to the house of David whose names include “Mighty God” and “Everlasting Father” (Isaiah 9:6), the first title used of the LORD himself in Isaiah 10:21. Micah promises a ruler from Bethlehem “whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity” (Micah 5:2), and Daniel sees “One like the Son of Man” coming with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14), a human figure who rides the clouds, which elsewhere only God does. Finally, the Wisdom of God appears in Proverbs 8 as a personified figure present with God at creation; the Hebrew verb in Proverbs 8:22 (qanah) can mean ‘acquire’, ‘possess’, or ‘create’, and the verse became a battleground in the Arian controversy. The New Testament's language for Christ as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2-3) draws on this Wisdom tradition.
nt:
Matthew and Luke tell of the conception. An angel tells Joseph that “the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20), and Matthew sees Isaiah's Immanuel fulfilled, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23). Luke's angel tells Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Both Gospels present the conception as a new act of God, not a human achievement, and the virginal conception is confessed in both the Apostles' and the Nicene creeds. The Gospels then show a fully human life. Jesus is born, grows “in wisdom and stature” (Luke 2:52), hungers after fasting (Matthew 4:2), sleeps in a boat (Mark 4:38), weeps at a friend's tomb (John 11:35), and says he does not know the day or the hour of the end (Mark 13:32). In Gethsemane he is “deeply troubled and distressed” and prays, “Yet not what I will, but what You will” (Mark 14:33, 36), a scene the church later cited to show that he has a real human will. The same Gospels show him forgiving sins, which his hearers rightly said only God can do (Mark 2:7), commanding the sea, and receiving worship. The disciples in the boat ask the question the doctrine answers: “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41).

John's Gospel states the doctrine most directly. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); all things were made through him; and this Word “became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), so that the glory once seen in the tabernacle is now seen in a man. Word (logos) was a term both Greek philosophers and Jewish writers such as Philo of Alexandria used for the rational principle or the self-expression of God, but John's Prologue echoes Genesis 1 and the Old Testament word and wisdom of God rather than a philosophical system. John 1:18 says “the one and only Son, who is Himself God” has made the Father known; the earliest papyri of John, P66 and P75, read ‘the only God’ here, while many later manuscripts read ‘the only Son’. Jesus later says, “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), speaks of the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed” (John 17:5), and calls his body a temple (John 2:21). Thomas's confession, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28), is the Gospel's climax.

Paul's letters, written earlier than the Gospels, already assume the doctrine. Christ is “a descendant of David according to the flesh” and declared Son of God with power by the resurrection (Romans 1:3-4); “God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law” (Galatians 4:4-5); God sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin” (Romans 8:3), a phrase that insists on real likeness without saying the Son sinned. The fullest passage is Philippians 2:5-11, which most scholars believe preserves an early Christian hymn or poem: Christ, “existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness” (Philippians 2:6-7), then humbled himself to death on a cross and was exalted to receive the name above every name. What the emptying means is debated (see below), but Paul uses it to urge humility, not to speculate. Paul also writes that “in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (Colossians 2:9), and that he became poor so that we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The mediator between God and humanity is “the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), a present-tense statement that the risen Christ remains human. In 1 Timothy 3:16 the church's confession begins, “He appeared in the flesh”; later manuscripts read ‘God was manifested in the flesh’, but the earliest, including Codex Sinaiticus, read ‘who’.

Hebrews binds the incarnation to salvation. The Son is “the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3), far above the angels, and yet “He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest” (Hebrews 2:17). He shared flesh and blood to destroy death by dying (Hebrews 2:14); he was “tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15); and “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). The letters of John make the incarnation a test of true teaching: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2), and those who refuse to confess it are deceivers (2 John 7). The first readers of 1 John were evidently facing teachers who denied that the divine Christ had truly come in a human body. The New Testament ends with the risen Jesus still embodied (Luke 24:39), ascended in the same body and coming again “in the same way” (Acts 1:11), and with the promise of the tabernacle fulfilled at last: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

keyTexts.why: The glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle. John 1:14 says the Word ‘tabernacled’ among us and that his glory was seen.
Solomon asks whether God will indeed dwell on earth, when heaven itself cannot contain him. The question the incarnation answers.
The sign of Immanuel, God with us. Matthew quotes the Septuagint's ‘virgin’ and sees its fullest meaning in Jesus' birth.
A child born to David's house is called Mighty God and will reign forever. Royal promise stretched beyond ordinary humanity.
One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus' favorite self-designation draws on this figure.
The Lord will suddenly come to his temple after his messenger prepares the way. The Gospels apply it to John the Baptist and Jesus.
Jesus is conceived by the Holy Spirit and named Immanuel. The virginal conception marks his birth as God's new act.
The Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High overshadow Mary, and the child will be called the Son of God.
Jesus grew in wisdom and stature. The incarnation included a real human childhood and development.
The Word who was God became flesh and dwelt among us. The church's primary text for the doctrine.
God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law. Preexistence and true birth in one sentence.
The one in the form of God emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was exalted. The source of the kenosis debate.
All the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ in bodily form. Deity not diminished by the body, and a body not erased by deity.
The Son shared flesh and blood and was made like his brothers in every way so that he could be a merciful high priest. Why the humanity matters for salvation.
Confessing that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is the test of the Spirit of God. The earliest rejection of docetism.

history:
The first Christian writers after the apostles had to defend the incarnation against people who found a truly human Christ unworthy of God. Ignatius of Antioch, writing letters on his way to martyrdom in Rome around 110, insisted against the Docetists (from dokein, ‘to seem’, who taught that Christ only seemed to have flesh) that Jesus was truly born, truly ate and drank, truly suffered and died. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies, around 180) argued that Christ became what we are so that he might bring us to be what he is, and Tertullian's On the Flesh of Christ (early third century) defended his real body. At the Council of Nicaea in 325, called by Constantine, the church confessed against Arius that the Son is of one substance (homoousios) with the Father, and that for us and our salvation he came down, was made flesh, and became man. Athanasius's On the Incarnation made the case that only God could restore his image in humanity and only a man could die humanity's death. When Apollinaris of Laodicea taught that the divine Word took the place of a human mind in Christ, Gregory of Nazianzus answered in his letters to Cledonius that what Christ did not assume he did not heal, and the Council of Constantinople in 381 condemned Apollinarianism.

The fifth century fought over how the two natures are united. Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople from 428, objected to calling Mary Theotokos, ‘God-bearer’, and was understood by his opponents to divide Christ into two subjects. Cyril of Alexandria insisted that the one born of Mary is the Son of God himself, and the Council of Ephesus in 431 deposed Nestorius; the Formula of Reunion of 433 brought Cyril and the Antiochene bishops to agreement. Eutyches, a monastic leader in Constantinople, then taught that after the union Christ had only one nature, and was condemned in 448, restored at the disputed council of Ephesus in 449, and condemned again at Chalcedon in 451. Chalcedon, receiving the Tome of Pope Leo I, confessed one and the same Christ, perfect in deity and perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, of one substance with the Father as to his deity and with us as to his humanity, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac, Armenian, and Malankara) did not accept Chalcedon's formula, preferring Cyril's language of one incarnate nature of the Word; they reject Eutyches and confess Christ fully God and fully man, and joint declarations such as that of Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III (10 May 1973) have recognized a shared faith in substance. The Church of the East, often called Nestorian, signed a Common Christological Declaration with the Catholic Church on 11 November 1994.

Later councils completed the picture. The Second Council of Constantinople (553) stressed that the one person of the natures is the eternal Son. When monothelitism taught that Christ had only one will, Maximus the Confessor (died 662) argued from Gethsemane that Christ had a real human will freely conformed to the divine, and the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681) confessed two wills and two operations, divine and human, in harmony. The Second Council of Nicaea (787), drawing on John of Damascus, defended icons on the ground that the invisible God had become visible in Christ. In the medieval West Anselm's Cur Deus Homo (1098) asked why the incarnation was necessary for redemption, and Thomas Aquinas and John Duns Scotus disagreed about whether it would have happened without the fall. At the Reformation, Lutherans and Reformed agreed on Chalcedon but divided over how the natures share their properties, a question tied to the Lord's Supper; the Formula of Concord (1577, Article VIII) and the Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Questions 47 and 48) state the two positions.

In the modern period, kenotic theologians in nineteenth-century Germany and Britain, among them Gottfried Thomasius and Charles Gore, proposed that the Son laid aside certain divine attributes in becoming man. Edward Irving was deposed from the Church of Scotland ministry in 1833 for teaching that Christ assumed fallen human nature, a view Karl Barth and T. F. Torrance later developed. Critical scholarship questioned whether the doctrine belongs to the New Testament at all; the collection The Myth of God Incarnate (1977), edited by John Hick, argued it was a later mythological development, and The Truth of God Incarnate, edited by Michael Green the same year, replied. Scholars of early Christian worship such as Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham have since argued that devotion to Jesus as divine arose very early among Jewish believers, within the first two decades after the crucifixion. The Western church has celebrated Christmas on 25 December since at least the fourth century (a Roman calendar of 354 records the feast for the year 336), and the Feast of the Annunciation on 25 March.

differ.view: Would the Son have become incarnate without the fall?
differ.body: Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae III, question 1, article 3) judged that, since Scripture everywhere gives the remedy of sin as the reason for the incarnation, it is more fitting to say the Son would not have become incarnate had humanity not sinned, while granting that God's power is not limited to that. John Duns Scotus and others following him held that Christ was willed first, as the goal of creation and the crown of God's works, and that the incarnation would have happened even without sin, the fall only determining that he came as a suffering redeemer. Defenders of Scotus's view point to Colossians 1:15-17 and Ephesians 1:9-10, where all things were created for Christ; defenders of Aquinas point to texts like Galatians 4:4-5 and 1 Timothy 1:15.

differ.view: Did the Son assume a fallen or an unfallen human nature?
differ.body: The majority of Christian teaching has held that the Son took a true human nature subject to weakness, suffering, and death, but not a nature corrupted by sin, since he was conceived by the Spirit and was “without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Its defenders, including Oliver Crisp among recent theologians, argue that a fallen nature would carry the guilt and corruption of original sin. Others, including Edward Irving, Karl Barth, and T. F. Torrance, have argued that the Son assumed human nature as it actually is after the fall, “in the likeness of sinful man” (Romans 8:3), and sanctified it from within by never sinning, so that nothing in our condition is left unhealed. Both sides confess that Christ never sinned.

Most classical interpreters read Philippians 2:7 as emptying by addition: the Son, remaining fully God, took the form of a servant, veiling his glory and choosing not to use his divine prerogatives independently of the Father's will. Kenotic theologians since the nineteenth century have argued that the Son actually laid aside the exercise, and in some versions the possession, of attributes such as omniscience and omnipotence during his earthly life, so that his human experience would be genuine; they point to Mark 13:32 and Luke 2:52. Critics answer that the stronger versions make God changeable. Many holding the classical view explain texts such as Mark 13:32 by distinguishing what the Son knows in his human mind from what he knows as God. The site's page on who Jesus is sets out this debate further.

differ.view: How do the natures share their properties? (Lutheran and Reformed)
differ.body: All orthodox Christians agree that what belongs to either nature can be said of the one person, so that it is right to say God was born of Mary and the Lord of glory was crucified. Lutheran theology, in the Formula of Concord, further teaches that the human nature, in union with the divine, truly shares in divine majesty, including a presence not limited to one place, which supports its teaching of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper. Reformed theology, in the Heidelberg Catechism and elsewhere, holds that the human nature remains finite and located, now in heaven, while the Son in his divinity is present everywhere and is not confined to his human body (the teaching Lutherans nicknamed the extra Calvinisticum). Both sides confess Chalcedon and accuse the other of drifting toward an ancient error, which each denies.

errors:
The early church rejected a series of positions, each of which protected one truth at the cost of another. Docetism denied that Christ had a real body, and 1 John 4:2-3 already rejects it. The Ebionites and later adoptionists held that Jesus was a man adopted as God's Son at his baptism or resurrection, not the eternal Son become man. Arianism, condemned at Nicaea (325), made the Son the first and highest creature, so that the one who became flesh was not God. Apollinarianism, condemned at Constantinople (381), gave Christ a human body but not a human mind. Nestorianism, as the Council of Ephesus (431) understood it, divided Christ into two subjects, a divine Son and a human Jesus joined by association. Eutychianism, rejected at Chalcedon (451), so merged the natures that the humanity was lost in the divinity. Monothelitism, rejected at Constantinople (680-681), denied Christ a human will. The Oriental Orthodox churches, which did not accept Chalcedon's wording, also reject Eutyches, and should not be identified with his teaching.

These are not ancient curiosities. Popular Christianity often slides into a practical docetism, a Jesus who only seemed to hunger, fear, and struggle, or a practical adoptionism, a Jesus admired as the best of men. Both miss the confession. The church's reasoning in each case was about salvation: if Christ is not truly God, then God has not come to rescue us; if he is not truly man, then our humanity has not been taken up and healed. Hebrews 2:17 states the logic in Scripture's own words.
life:
The incarnation means that God is not a distant idea but has a face and a name. When Christians ask what God is like, they look at Jesus, who said that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). The doctrine also dignifies ordinary human life. The Son spent most of his years in a small town, working with his hands, in a family, under the law, and he took all of it, body and mind, into union with himself. Nothing human is beneath God's notice, and the body is not a prison to escape but part of what God made good and came to redeem.

For prayer and suffering, the incarnation means that the one to whom believers pray has been where they are. Hebrews says he can “sympathize with our weaknesses” because he was tempted in every way as we are (Hebrews 4:15), and because he suffered when tempted, “He is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). He still bears a human nature in heaven, so the hope of Christians is not escape from being human but the renewal of human life, soul and body, in the likeness of the risen Christ. And the pattern of his coming, the rich one becoming poor for the sake of others (2 Corinthians 8:9), is held out by Paul as the pattern for how Christians treat one another (Philippians 2:5).
questions: The Old Testament tells of God dwelling in the tabernacle and temple. How does John 1:14 build on that story, and what does it suggest about where God is to be found now?
The Gospels show Jesus hungry, tired, grieving, and not knowing the hour, and also forgiving sins and calming storms. Why did the early church insist on holding both sides together in one person?
Hebrews 2:17-18 says Christ had to be made like us in every way. Which part of your own experience is it hardest to believe he shared, and what difference would it make if he did?
